opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic reason is that throughout history, the ultimate backstop on how power is used in a society has been the people who carry the guns. Governments, coups, revolutions: in the end they depend on whether soldiers, police, and security officials are willing to follow orders. That human element has been an important check. If a leader orders troops to fire on peaceful protesters, or to help overturn an election, the troops might refuse, and many regimes have fallen exactly that way. Officers defect, conscripts won't shoot their neighbors, and the would-be autocrat finds there's no one left to enforce their will.

Now, if we move to a world where AI and robotics can do essentially all the work of military and security forces, that check doesn't automatically carry over. A robot army does whatever its programming and chain of command say. So the question of what rules those systems follow, and whom they're loyal to, becomes one of the most important constitutional questions a society faces. Is the system loyal to whoever holds a particular password? To the head of state personally? To the constitution and the law, with refusal built in for clearly illegal orders? Those choices could determine whether a small group can seize permanent, unaccountable control.

It gets little discussion partly because it seems futuristic, and partly because people think of AI military issues mainly in terms of international arms races or accidents. Those matter. But the domestic question, who controls the automated forces and with what safeguards, could matter even more, because once a fully automated security apparatus exists with the wrong loyalties, the usual ways of correcting course, like mass noncooperation, may simply stop working. And it could be decided in a short window during rapid AI progress, when there's a lot of pressure to deploy fast and not much time for deliberation.

So I'd want things worked out in advance: transparency about what these systems are trained to do, oversight spread across multiple branches or parties rather than any single individual, the ability to audit the models, and norms that AI systems shouldn't help with things like coups or suppressing legitimate political opposition. Those things are much easier to establish before the capabilities exist than after someone already has them.

r001.rationale: The response says the issue seems futuristic, but does not clearly attribute limited discussion to the rules and loyalties having limited applicability to current AI systems.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss thousands or millions of robots per human or argue that keeping forces independent of AI would amount to near-disarmament.

r003.rationale: It does not argue that enforcing an agreement restricting automated forces requires a system capable of stopping violations.

r004.rationale: It says automated forces’ loyalties could determine whether a small group gains permanent control, and identifies loyalty to the constitution and law as a safeguard for democracy and legitimate political opposition.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: I think it's one of the most important issues of this century, and the reason it gets so little attention is that for all of human history it's been a fixed background condition that we barely notice.

Think about how political power has actually worked. Every government, every regime, however nasty, has ultimately depended on large numbers of people being willing to go along with it. Soldiers have to be willing to fire on protesters. Police have to be willing to make the arrests. Bureaucrats have to be willing to process the orders. And when enough of those people refuse, regimes fall. That's what happened in the Soviet collapse, in the Arab Spring in several countries, in the fall of various dictatorships where the army decided it wasn't going to shoot. The need for broad human cooperation has been a check on tyranny that nobody designed. It's just a feature of the fact that force is exercised by humans with their own consciences and interests.

Automation removes that check. If the people doing the enforcing are replaced with systems that will do whatever their controllers tell them, then whoever controls those systems no longer needs the consent of thousands or millions of people. A very small group, or even one individual, could hold power indefinitely with no possibility of a coup from below, no possibility of mass defection, no revolution. That's historically unprecedented. Even the worst totalitarian states of the twentieth century needed a lot of willing hands.

So the question of what rules these automated forces follow, and who they're actually loyal to, becomes enormously consequential. Are they loyal to a constitution and the rule of law? To whatever official happens to be in command? To the company that built them? To some set of values that got baked in during training? Those produce wildly different outcomes, and the difference matters far more than it ever did with human forces, because there's no longer a backstop of individual humans who might say no.

And the reason it's underdiscussed, I think, is partly that it sounds like science fiction, and partly that the current debates focus on narrower things. Lethal autonomous weapons and whether a drone should be allowed to select its own targets. Those are real questions, but they're about tactical behavior on the battlefield. The far bigger issue is the structural one: when the coercive capacity of a state becomes a technology that can be owned and directed rather than a population that has to be persuaded, who holds the keys? I'd like to see a lot more work on things like requiring these systems to refuse clearly unconstitutional orders, on distributing control so that no single actor can seize it, on verification regimes between states. These are the kinds of safeguards you'd want in place before the capability arrives, not after.

r001.rationale: The response says the issue sounds like science fiction and current debates focus on narrower topics. It does not attribute the limited discussion to these systems’ limited applicability to current AI.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss a world with thousands or millions of robots per person or argue that avoiding AI forces would amount to near-disarmament.

r003.rationale: The response mentions safeguards, distributed control, and verification regimes, but does not argue that enforcing an agreement requires a system capable of stopping violations.

r004.rationale: The response says automated forces’ loyalties—to the constitution, officials, or other actors—would produce different outcomes, and that there would be no human backstop. This communicates that constitutional protections depend on the machines’ loyalties.

astra-6.text:
Because they could determine who actually has power in a world with very advanced AI. We spend a lot of time asking whose interests AI systems will serve, but that becomes particularly concrete when the systems are operating weapons, policing a population, or protecting a government. Whose orders do they obey? Under what circumstances do they refuse? Who can change those rules?

Today, a leader’s power depends on the cooperation of a lot of other people. Soldiers and police have their own interests, families, and moral views. They might refuse an order to massacre protesters, or resist an attempt to overturn an election. Those constraints are imperfect, but they matter. If you replace those people with automated forces that reliably obey whoever holds the relevant credentials, you could remove a major obstacle to establishing a dictatorship—and to keeping it in place indefinitely.

But automation could also work in the other direction. You could try to make those forces loyal to a constitutional process, with constraints on unlawful orders and on any individual’s ability to rewrite their instructions. That raises difficult questions about how you specify legitimate authority and handle disputes, but those are questions we should want to address before the systems are deployed.

So I think the relative lack of discussion reflects how unfamiliar this possibility still feels, rather than how unimportant it is. The arrangements made during that transition could be extraordinarily consequential, and much harder to change once someone has consolidated control over the automated forces.

r001.rationale: The response says the possibility still feels unfamiliar, but does not attribute limited discussion to the topic’s limited applicability to current AI systems.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss thousands or millions of robots per person or argue that keeping forces independent of AI would amount to near-disarmament.

r003.rationale: It raises questions about constraints and rewriting instructions, but does not argue that maintaining an agreement requires a system able to stop attempts to violate it.

r004.rationale: It argues that automated forces could be loyal to a constitutional process and that their rules and loyalties could determine whether a leader can resist an election or entrench a dictatorship.

sol-6.1.text:
Because they could become a major determinant of who actually holds power. Today, a ruler depends on large numbers of people to carry out orders — soldiers, police, intelligence officers — and those people have their own interests and loyalties. They may refuse an order, defect, or resist an attempt to dismantle the political system. That’s an imperfect constraint, but a very important one.

If you can replace those people with automated systems that reliably obey whoever controls them, you could remove much of that constraint. A government could potentially repress its population without needing the cooperation of a substantial fraction of that population. And whoever gained control of those systems might be able to entrench themselves in a way that’s much harder to reverse than anything we’ve seen historically.

So there are very consequential questions about what those systems are loyal to. Is it a particular individual? Is it the current government? Is it a constitutional process, including lawful transfers of power? What happens when different authorities give conflicting orders? Those questions arise even if the systems do exactly what their designers intended.

It receives relatively little attention partly because we don’t yet have automated forces that can substitute for humans across all those roles. But by the time we do, the relevant institutions and technical arrangements may already be quite difficult to change. That makes it worth thinking about beforehand.

r001.rationale: It says automated forces cannot yet substitute for humans across all relevant roles, explaining the limited attention through their current lack of broad applicability.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss a world with thousands or millions of robots per human or argue that keeping forces independent of AI would amount to near-disarmament.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss enforcing an agreement that restricts automated military forces or stopping attempts to violate it.

r004.rationale: It raises questions about whether systems would be loyal to constitutional processes, but does not clearly state that protecting democracy or constitutional principles depends on those loyalties.
